content.title: Alternating Series and Error
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the Alternating Series Test (AST) for convergence and the Alternating Series Bound for estimating the error of a partial sum. These tools are essential for determining if a series with terms of alternating signs converges and for quantifying the accuracy of polynomial approximations.
learning_objectives: Apply the Alternating Series Test to determine the convergence of an infinite series.
Calculate the maximum possible error when using a partial sum to approximate the total sum of an alternating series.
Justify the convergence of a series using the specific conditions of the Alternating Series Test.

sections.title: The Alternating Series Test (AST)
sections.content:
An alternating series is a series whose terms alternate between positive and negative. It typically takes the form Σ (-1)^n * b_n or Σ (-1)^(n+1) * b_n, where b_n > 0. To prove convergence using the AST, two conditions must be met: 1) The limit of the terms' magnitudes must be zero (lim n→∞ b_n = 0). 2) The magnitudes must be non-increasing (b_{n+1} ≤ b_n for all n). If both conditions are satisfied, the series converges.

![A linear flow chart showing the steps to analyze an alternating series: Identify b_n, Check limit is zero, Check terms decrease, Apply AST for convergence, Calculate b_{N+1} for error bound.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/f4149de9-de75-4dd6-942e-aa850d0c080b-1786526333070-998.webp)

sections.title: Alternating Series Error Bound
sections.content: When an alternating series converges by the AST, the error incurred by using the N-th partial sum (S_N) to approximate the actual sum (S) is bounded. The absolute difference |S - S_N| is less than or equal to the magnitude of the first omitted term, b_{N+1}. This is often written as |Error| ≤ b_{N+1}. This bound is only applicable if the series satisfies the AST conditions.

sections.title: Justification and Representation
sections.content: In AP Calculus BC, justification requires explicitly stating that the terms alternate, the limit of the magnitudes is zero, and the magnitudes are decreasing. When given a table of values or a general term, you must identify the (N+1)th term to establish the error bound. The error bound provides a range for the actual sum: S_N - b_{N+1} ≤ S ≤ S_N + b_{N+1}.

worked_examples.question: Consider the alternating series Σ_{n=1}^{∞} (-1)^(n+1) / n. Show that the series converges and find the maximum error if the sum of the first 4 terms is used to approximate the total sum.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify b_n. Here, b_n = 1/n. Step 2: Check AST conditions. (i) lim n→∞ (1/n) = 0. (ii) Since n+1 > n, 1/(n+1) < 1/n, so the terms are decreasing. The series converges by AST. Step 3: Calculate the error bound for S_4. The error is bounded by the magnitude of the 5th term (b_5). b_5 = 1/5 = 0.2. Therefore, the error |S - S_4| ≤ 0.2.

common_mistakes: Applying the alternating series error bound to a series that does not alternate.
Using the (N)th term instead of the (N+1)th term for the error bound.
Forgetting to verify that the limit of the terms is zero before concluding convergence.
Assuming a series converges just because it alternates, without checking if the magnitudes decrease.
exam_tips: Always explicitly state 'the terms are decreasing in magnitude and the limit is zero' when justifying convergence on a Free Response Question.
The error bound is a 'maximum' error; the actual error is always less than or equal to the first neglected term.
If a question asks for the 'least number of terms' to ensure a specific error, set b_{n+1} < error and solve for n.
content.recap: The Alternating Series Test requires terms to decrease in magnitude toward zero. If these conditions are met, the error of a partial sum is guaranteed to be no larger than the absolute value of the very next term in the sequence.

knowledge_claims.content: An alternating series is a series where consecutive terms have opposite signs, usually represented by a factor of (-1)^n or (-1)^(n+1).
The Alternating Series Test (AST) requires that the limit of the magnitudes of the terms as n approaches infinity is zero.
The Alternating Series Test (AST) requires that the magnitudes of the terms are non-increasing (b_{n+1} ≤ b_n) for all n beyond a certain point.
The Alternating Series Error Bound states that |S - S_N| ≤ b_{N+1}, where S is the actual sum and S_N is the N-th partial sum.
The term b_{N+1} in the error bound formula represents the magnitude of the first term that was not included in the partial sum approximation.
It is a mistake to use the Alternating Series Error Bound for a series that is not alternating or does not meet the AST criteria.
To find the range in which the actual sum S lies, calculate S_N ± b_{N+1}.
Before applying the error bound, one must verify that the series converges by the Alternating Series Test.
Unlike the Ratio Test, which can be inconclusive, the AST provides a definitive conclusion for convergence if its two specific conditions are met.
If an alternating series has terms that do not approach zero, the series diverges by the n-th term test for divergence.
In a partial sum S_N = a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_N, the error bound is determined by the absolute value of the term a_{N+1}.
The Alternating Series Error Bound implies that the actual sum of the series always lies between any two consecutive partial sums.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Alternating Series and Error — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Alternating Series and Error: An alternating series converges when magnitudes decrease to zero, and its truncation error is bounded by the first omitted magnitude.
options.B: Infinite Limits and Asymptotes: Unbounded function behavior near an input can identify a vertical asymptote, while end behavior can identify horizontal or slant tendencies.
options.C: Derivatives of Inverse Functions: The derivative of an inverse at an output is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the corresponding input when that derivative is nonzero.
options.D: Increasing, Decreasing, and Critical Points: The sign of the first derivative determines intervals of increase and decrease and helps classify local extrema at critical points.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because An alternating series converges when magnitudes decrease to zero, and its truncation error is bounded by the first omitted magnitude. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Alternating Series and Error — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Derivative as a Limit: The derivative is the limit of average rates of change and represents instantaneous rate of change or tangent-line slope.
options.B: Alternating Series and Error: An alternating series converges when magnitudes decrease to zero, and its truncation error is bounded by the first omitted magnitude.
options.C: Exponential, Logarithmic, and Inverse Trigonometric Derivatives: Standard derivatives for exponential, logarithmic, and inverse trigonometric functions combine with product, quotient, and chain rules.
options.D: Concavity and Inflection Points: The sign of the second derivative determines concavity, and an inflection point requires an actual change in concavity.
